decks.title: Quantum Mechanical Model and Electronic Configuration — Part 1: wave function, quantum numbers and orbitals
goals: Explain what the wave function ψ and ψ² mean and what is meant by an orbital
Use the four quantum numbers to describe an electron and count shells, subshells, orbitals and electrons
Describe the shapes, sizes and orientations of s, p and d orbitals and calculate their radial and angular nodes

slides.heading: The quantum mechanical model of the atom
slides.body_md: Part 1: how a wave equation replaces the orbit, what the quantum numbers say, and what orbitals look like.

slides.narration: Welcome. Bohr pictured the electron as a particle on a fixed circular path, but the uncertainty principle showed that cannot be right. In this part we meet the wave equation that replaced it, the four quantum numbers that come out of it, and the shapes and nodes of the orbitals.

slides.heading: From orbit to orbital
slides.body_md: A **Bohr orbit** is a fixed circular path. An **orbital** is a region of space around the nucleus where the electron is **most likely to be found**, described by a **wave function**. The new model treats the electron as a wave and gives only **probabilities**.

rows: Wave described by a wave function ψ
Only a probability of being found
Three, n, l and mₗ, plus spin

visual.alt: Table comparing a Bohr orbit with a quantum mechanical orbital

slides.narration: An orbit is a fixed circular path. An orbital is quite different. It is a region of space around the nucleus in which the electron is most likely to be found, and it is described by a wave function. The model gives only probabilities, needs three quantum numbers instead of one, and applies to every atom.

slides.heading: The Schrödinger wave equation (no derivation)
slides.body_md: Schrödinger wrote an equation that treats the electron as a matter wave: $$\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$$ Here $\hat{H}$ is the **Hamiltonian operator** (kinetic plus potential energy), $E$ is the **energy** and $\psi$ is the **wave function**. It has acceptable solutions only for **certain values of $E$**. For hydrogen it can be solved exactly; for many-electron atoms only approximately.

nodes.label: Write the equation for the electron in the field of the nucleus
Solve it: only some energies E give acceptable wave functions
Each solution ψ is labelled by n, l and mₗ
Each ψ is one orbital with its own energy and shape

visual.alt: Flow chart from the Schrödinger equation to the allowed wave functions labelled by quantum numbers

slides.narration: Schrödinger wrote one equation for the electron as a matter wave. It links the wave function to the energy through the Hamiltonian operator. Acceptable solutions exist only for certain energies, and each solution is labelled by whole numbers called quantum numbers. We do not derive it. Exact solutions exist for hydrogen, and approximate ones for larger atoms.

slides.heading: What ψ and ψ² mean
slides.body_md: The wave function $\psi$ has **no direct physical meaning**. The **square of its magnitude, $\psi^2$**, at a point is the **probability density**: the probability of finding the electron in a tiny volume there is $\psi^2 \times$ volume. Over all space the total probability is **1**. Where $\psi^2 = 0$, the electron is **never** found.

rows: Probability of finding the electron in that volume
Probability in a thin shell at distance r

visual.alt: Table of the meaning of ψ, ψ², probability in a volume and radial probability

slides.narration: The wave function itself has no direct physical meaning. Its square does. At any point, the square of the wave function is the probability density, so multiplying it by a small volume gives the chance of finding the electron there. The total probability over all space is one, and where the square is zero the electron is never found.

slides.heading: Seeing the probability: the 1s electron
slides.body_md: The dots crowd where **ψ² is large**, close to the nucleus. The **radial probability** $4\pi r^2\psi^2$ includes the growing volume of each shell, so it is zero at the nucleus and peaks at **$1\,a_0$**. A **boundary surface** encloses about **90%** of the probability.

slides.narration: Each dot is one snapshot of where the electron might be. They crowd near the nucleus where the density is greatest, and thin out with distance. slides.heading: Quick check: what ψ² tells us
slides.body_md: Decide what the square of the wave function gives at a point.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that the wave function itself is only an amplitude and may be positive or negative. Think about which quantity can be interpreted as a probability per unit volume, and which quantity can never be negative, then choose the statement that matches.

slides.heading: Orbital and boundary surface
slides.body_md: An **orbital** is the wave function of one electron in an atom; each orbital has its own **energy, shape and size**. Because ψ² never drops exactly to zero, a **boundary surface diagram** is drawn to contain about **90% of the probability**. An orbital holds **at most two electrons**.

rows: One-electron wave function ψ, with fixed energy
Region where the electron is found about 90% of the time
ψ² falls off with distance but never becomes exactly zero

visual.alt: Table summarising the idea of an orbital and the boundary surface

slides.narration: An orbital is the wave function of one electron, and each orbital has its own energy, shape and size. Because the probability fades away with distance but never reaches exactly zero, we draw a boundary surface that contains about ninety percent of the probability. Each orbital can hold at most two electrons.

slides.heading: The four quantum numbers
slides.body_md: Solving the wave equation gives three quantum numbers; a fourth describes **spin**. $n$ = 1, 2, 3 … ; $l$ = 0 to $n-1$; $m_l$ = $-l$ to $+l$ (that is $2l+1$ values); $m_s$ = $+\tfrac12$ or $-\tfrac12$. No two electrons in an atom can have the same four.

visual.alt: Table of the four quantum numbers with symbol, allowed values and meaning

slides.narration: There are four quantum numbers. The principal quantum number n labels the shell and fixes its size and energy. The azimuthal number l runs from zero to n minus one and labels the subshell and the shape. The magnetic number runs from minus l to plus l and gives the orientation. The spin number is plus or minus one half.

slides.heading: Shells, subshells and orbitals
slides.body_md: Each value of $l$ is a subshell: $l = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are **s, p, d, f**. A subshell has $2l+1$ orbitals: **1, 3, 5, 7**. Shell $n$ has **$n^2$ orbitals** and holds **$2n^2$ electrons**.

visual.caption: n² orbitals and 2n² electrons in shell n.

slides.narration: Here are the first four shells. The first shell has only an s orbital. The second has an s and three p orbitals. The third adds five d orbitals, and the fourth adds seven f orbitals. Shell number n therefore contains n squared orbitals, and since each holds two electrons, it holds up to two n squared electrons.

slides.heading: Worked example: quantum numbers of the 3p electrons
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** List every set of $(n, l, m_l, m_s)$ for the electrons that can occupy the $3p$ subshell, and say how many electrons it holds.

For $3p$: $n = 3$, $l = 1$, so $m_l = -1, 0, +1$ (three orbitals). Each orbital takes $m_s = +\tfrac12$ or $-\tfrac12$.

Sets: (3, 1, −1, +½), (3, 1, −1, −½), (3, 1, 0, +½), (3, 1, 0, −½), (3, 1, +1, +½), (3, 1, +1, −½).

Number of electrons $= 2(2l+1) = 2 \times 3 = 6$.

visual.alt: Table of the quantum numbers and electron capacity of the 3p subshell

slides.narration: For three p, n is three and l is one. So the magnetic quantum number can be minus one, zero or plus one, which means three orbitals. Each orbital can hold an electron with spin plus one half and another with spin minus one half. That gives six distinct sets of four quantum numbers, and six electrons in the subshell.

slides.heading: What the quantum numbers tell us
slides.body_md: **Distance and size:** a larger $n$ means the electron is **farther from the nucleus** on average and the orbital is **larger**. **Energy:** rises with $n$ (in many-electron atoms also with $l$). **Shape:** $l$. **Orientation:** $m_l$. **Electrons:** orbital 2, subshell $2(2l+1)$, shell $2n^2$.

rows: s sphere, p dumbbell, d clover

visual.alt: Table of what each quantum number tells about distance, energy, shape, orientation and electron count

slides.narration: Each quantum number tells us something. A larger principal quantum number means the electron is on average farther from the nucleus, the orbital is larger and the energy is higher. The azimuthal number gives the shape and the magnetic number the orientation. Counting rules then give the electrons: two in an orbital, and two n squared in a shell.

slides.heading: Quick check: allowed quantum numbers
slides.body_md: Test each set against the rules for n, l, mₗ and mₛ.
slides.narration: Quick check. For each set, first confirm that l is smaller than n. Then check that the magnetic number lies between minus l and plus l. Finally check that the spin number is plus or minus one half. Only a set that passes all three tests is allowed, so look for the single flaw in the wrong sets.

slides.heading: Shapes of s and p orbitals; size and orientation
slides.body_md: An **s orbital** ($l = 0$) is **spherical**. A **p orbital** ($l = 1$) has **two lobes** of opposite sign with a **nodal plane** through the nucleus; the three p orbitals point along **x, y and z**. For the same type, a higher shell means a **larger** orbital (3p > 2p, 3s > 2s > 1s).

visual.caption: Size grows with n; three p orbitals along three axes.

slides.narration: An s orbital is a sphere, and it gets larger as n increases. A p orbital has two lobes, one on each side of the nucleus, separated by a nodal plane where the electron is never found. The three p orbitals of a shell lie along the three axes at right angles, which is why there are exactly three of them.

slides.heading: The five d orbitals
slides.body_md: A **d orbital** ($l = 2$) has **two angular nodes**. Four of the five have **four lobes**: $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{xz}$ lie **between** the axes and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ lies **along** the axes. $d_{z^2}$ has **two lobes on the z axis and a ring** in the xy plane.

visual.alt: Cross-sections of the five d orbitals with their nodal planes and cones shown dashed
visual.caption: Five d orbitals, two angular nodes each.

slides.narration: Here are the five d orbitals. Three of them, d x y, d y z and d x z, have four lobes lying between the axes. The d x squared minus y squared orbital has four lobes along the x and y axes. The d z squared orbital has two lobes on the z axis and a ring around the middle. Each has two angular nodes.

slides.heading: Nodes: radial and angular
slides.body_md: A **node** is a place where $\psi^2 = 0$. **Radial nodes** are spherical surfaces at fixed distances: **$n - l - 1$**. **Angular nodes** are planes or cones through the nucleus: **$l$**. **Total nodes** $= (n - l - 1) + l = $ **$n - 1$**.

visual.alt: Table of radial, angular and total nodes for 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p and 3d

slides.narration: A node is a place where the probability of finding the electron is exactly zero. Radial nodes are spherical surfaces, and their number is n minus l minus one. Angular nodes are planes or cones through the nucleus, and their number equals l. Adding the two gives the total number of nodes, which is always n minus one.

slides.heading: Radial probability curves
slides.body_md: Each **peak** is a region of high probability; each **dip to zero** is a radial node. The most probable distances are **1.0** ($1s$), **4.0** ($2p$) and **9.0** ($3d$) in units of $a_0$. Number of peaks $=$ radial nodes $+ 1$.

visual.alt: Radial probability curves for 1s, 2s, 3s, 2p, 3p and 3d showing radial nodes as dashed red lines
visual.caption: Radial nodes = n − l − 1.

slides.narration: These curves show the chance of finding the electron at each distance from the nucleus. Where a curve touches zero, there is a radial node. The one s curve has no node and one peak. Two s has one node and two peaks. Three s has two nodes and three peaks. The number of peaks is always the number of radial nodes plus one.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting nodes
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the radial, angular and total nodes of the $4d$, $5p$ and $3s$ orbitals.

**$4d$:** $n = 4$, $l = 2$. Radial $= 4 - 2 - 1 = 1$; angular $= 2$; total $= 4 - 1 = 3$.

**$5p$:** radial $= 5 - 1 - 1 = 3$; angular $= 1$; total $= 4$.

**$3s$:** radial $= 3 - 0 - 1 = 2$; angular $= 0$; total $= 2$.

visual.alt: Table of the nodes of 4d, 5p and 3s orbitals

slides.narration: Use the rule that radial nodes equal n minus l minus one, and angular nodes equal l. For four d, that is one radial and two angular nodes, three in all. For five p it is three radial and one angular, four in all. For three s there are two radial nodes and no angular node, two in all.

slides.heading: Quick check: nodes in an orbital
slides.body_md: Use radial nodes = n − l − 1 and angular nodes = l.
slides.narration: Quick check. Read off the shell number and the subshell letter from the orbital name, and convert the letter into a value of l. Then apply the rule for radial nodes, and add the angular nodes if the question asks for the total. Check that your total equals n minus one.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: ψ has no physical meaning; ψ² is the probability density; an orbital is a one-electron wave function holding at most two electrons.
Quantum numbers: n (size, energy), l = 0 to n − 1 (shape), mₗ = −l to +l (orientation), mₛ = ±½ (spin).
Shell n: n² orbitals, 2n² electrons. Subshell: 2l + 1 orbitals, 2(2l + 1) electrons.
Nodes: radial n − l − 1, angular l, total n − 1.

rows: Four lobes or lobes and ring

visual.alt: Summary table of subshells with shape, number of orbitals and electron capacity

slides.narration: Summing up Part 1. The wave function has no direct meaning but its square is a probability density. An orbital is a one-electron wave function. The four quantum numbers fix size, shape, orientation and spin. A shell has n squared orbitals and two n squared electrons, and the number of radial and angular nodes follows from n and l.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Say "probability density" for ψ²; never say that ψ itself is a probability.
Always check l < n and −l ≤ mₗ ≤ +l before accepting a set of quantum numbers.
Radial nodes n − l − 1, angular nodes l, total n − 1: show the substitution.
Sketch p orbitals as two lobes with the nodal plane marked, and label the axis.
Do not call an orbital an orbit: an orbital is a region of probability.

rows: Counting n orbitals in shell n
Forgetting the spin number in a set

visual.alt: Table of common slips in Part 1 and how to fix them

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Describe the square of the wave function as a probability density. Before you accept a set of quantum numbers, check that l is less than n and that the magnetic number lies between minus l and plus l. Show the substitution when counting nodes, and never confuse an orbital with an orbit.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. Now that we know the orbitals, we can ask how electrons are placed in them. Three rules decide the ground state of an atom: the Aufbau principle for the order of energy, Pauli’s principle for how many electrons an orbital holds, and Hund’s rule for how electrons spread over equal orbitals.

slides.heading: Aufbau principle
slides.body_md: The German word *Aufbau* means building up. In the **ground state**, electrons occupy the **lowest-energy orbitals available first**. In a many-electron atom the energy depends on **both $n$ and $l$**, so a subshell of a higher shell can lie below one of a lower shell (4s below 3d).

nodes.label: Take the next electron of the atom
Find the vacant subshell of lowest energy
Place the electron there, obeying Pauli and Hund
Repeat until all Z electrons are placed

visual.alt: Flow chart of the Aufbau procedure for filling electrons one at a time into the lowest vacant orbital

slides.narration: Aufbau is a German word meaning building up. In the ground state, electrons go into the lowest-energy orbitals that are free. In a hydrogen atom the energy depends only on n, but in a many-electron atom it depends on n and l together, so a subshell of a higher shell can sit below a subshell of a lower shell.

slides.heading: The (n + l) rule
slides.body_md: Subshells fill in order of **increasing $(n + l)$**. If two subshells have the **same $(n + l)$**, the one with the **lower $n$** fills first.

visual.alt: Table applying the (n + l) rule to 4s, 3d, 4p and 5s

slides.narration: The n plus l rule says that subshells fill in order of increasing value of n plus l. When two subshells have the same value, the one with the lower n fills first. So four s, with a value of four, fills before three d, which has five. Three d then fills before four p, and four p before five s.

slides.heading: The order of filling
slides.body_md: Reading the numbers in the boxes gives the order: **1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p**. Arrows join subshells of equal $(n + l)$.

Each coloured arrow joins subshells with the same n plus l, and electrons go first to the one at the top of the arrow. This is the sequence you should learn for writing configurations.

slides.heading: Worked example: arranging subshells by energy
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange $4f$, $5s$, $6s$, $4d$ and $5p$ in order of increasing energy.

$(n+l)$ values: $4f = 4+3 = 7$; $5s = 5+0 = 5$; $6s = 6+0 = 6$; $4d = 4+2 = 6$; $5p = 5+1 = 6$.

$5s$ has the lowest value. $4d$, $5p$, $6s$ all have 6, so they go by $n$: $4d < 5p < 6s$. $4f$ (7) is highest.

Order: 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f.

visual.alt: Table ranking 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s and 4f by the (n + l) rule

slides.narration: Calculate n plus l for each. Five s gives five, so it is lowest. Four d, five p and six s all give six, so they are ordered by n: four d first, then five p, then six s. Four f gives seven and is highest. The order is five s, four d, five p, six s, four f.

slides.heading: Quick check: the order of subshells
slides.body_md: Work out n + l for each subshell and use n to break ties.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write n plus l next to each subshell in the question. Put the smallest value first. If two subshells share a value, put the one with the smaller shell number first. Then compare the order you have found with the options, one at a time.

slides.heading: Pauli’s exclusion principle
slides.body_md: No two electrons in an atom can have **all four quantum numbers the same**. Two electrons in one orbital share $n$, $l$, $m_l$, so they must differ in $m_s$: **an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins**. This gives shell capacity $2n^2$.

visual.alt: Table of the maximum number of electrons in an orbital, subshells and a shell from Pauli’s principle

slides.narration: Pauli’s exclusion principle says that no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same. Two electrons in the same orbital already share the first three, so they must have opposite spins, and a third electron cannot fit. That is why an orbital holds two electrons and a shell holds two n squared.

slides.heading: Hund’s rule of maximum multiplicity
slides.body_md: In a subshell of **equal-energy orbitals**, electrons occupy **separate orbitals with parallel spins first**; pairing begins only when every orbital has one electron. Singly filled orbitals keep electrons apart (**less repulsion**) and give the **greatest number of unpaired electrons**.

visual.alt: Table showing Hund’s rule for one to six electrons in a p subshell with the number of unpaired electrons

slides.narration: Hund’s rule applies when a subshell has several orbitals of equal energy. Electrons go into separate orbitals with parallel spins first, and pair up only when every orbital in the subshell already holds one electron. This keeps the electrons apart, lowers the repulsion, and gives the largest number of unpaired electrons.

slides.heading: Orbital box diagrams
slides.body_md: Phosphorus: $3s^2\,3p^3$ gives **three unpaired** electrons (Hund). Iron has **four**; Fe³⁺ has **five** (half-filled 3d). Chromium has **six** and copper **one**. Each box holds an up-arrow and a down-arrow at most (Pauli).

visual.alt: Orbital box diagrams of P, Fe, Fe3+, Cr and Cu showing paired and unpaired electrons
visual.caption: Hund: singly first. Pauli: two per box at most.

slides.narration: In these diagrams each box is an orbital and each arrow an electron. Phosphorus has three unpaired electrons in its three p boxes, as Hund’s rule requires. Iron has four unpaired. The iron three plus ion has five. Chromium has six and copper just one. No box ever holds more than two arrows, as Pauli requires.

slides.heading: Worked example: orbital diagram of sulfur
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the configuration of sulfur ($Z = 16$), draw the $3p$ boxes, and give the number of unpaired electrons and a set of quantum numbers for the last electron.

Configuration: $1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{4}$, or $[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^4$.

$3p^4$: three boxes get one electron each, the fourth electron pairs in the first box: $\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$, so **2 unpaired**.

Last electron (by convention $m_l = -1$ fills first, then pairs): $(3, 1, -1, -\tfrac12)$.

visual.alt: Table of the orbital filling of sulfur in 3s and 3p

slides.narration: Sulfur has sixteen electrons, so after the neon core it has two in three s and four in three p. The first three p electrons go singly into the three boxes. The fourth must pair with the first. That leaves two unpaired electrons. By convention the last electron has n three, l one, magnetic number minus one, and spin minus one half.

slides.heading: Quick check: unpaired electrons
slides.body_md: Write the configuration, then apply Hund’s rule to the outer subshell.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the full configuration of the atom or ion first, using the order of filling. Identify the outermost partly filled subshell and draw its boxes. Place electrons singly before pairing them, then count how many boxes hold a single arrow. Complete subshells contribute no unpaired electrons.

slides.heading: Writing electronic configurations
slides.body_md: Fill subshells in the **Aufbau order** until Z electrons are placed, then write them in order of **increasing $n$** (3d before 4s). The **noble-gas core** shortens the notation: $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2$. Elements **Z = 21 to 30** show the 3d series; **Cr and Cu** are exceptions.

visual.alt: Table of the configurations of the elements from scandium to zinc with unpaired electrons

slides.narration: To write a configuration, fill the subshells in the order of increasing n plus l until you have placed all the electrons, and then write them grouped by shell. A noble gas symbol in brackets can replace the inner core. The table shows scandium to zinc. Notice that chromium and copper do not follow the simple order.

slides.heading: Chromium and copper: extra stability
slides.body_md: Cr should be $3d^4\,4s^2$ but is **$3d^5\,4s^1$**; Cu should be $3d^9\,4s^2$ but is **$3d^{10}\,4s^1$**. **Half-filled** ($d^5$) and **completely filled** ($d^{10}$) subshells are **extra stable**: symmetrical distribution and **greater exchange energy**, and 4s and 3d are close in energy so one 4s electron shifts.

visual.alt: Table comparing the expected and actual configurations of chromium and copper

slides.narration: Chromium and copper are the two exceptions up to zinc. Chromium would be three d four, four s two, but moves one electron to give three d five, four s one. Copper moves one electron to give a full three d ten. Half-filled and completely filled subshells are extra stable, because of symmetry and greater exchange energy.

slides.heading: Worked example: cobalt and its ions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the configurations of Co ($Z = 27$), Co²⁺ and Co³⁺, and give the unpaired electrons.

**Co:** [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s², 3 unpaired.

Cations lose electrons from the **outermost shell first**, so the $4s$ electrons go before $3d$.

**Co²⁺:** remove both $4s$: [Ar] 3d⁷, 3 unpaired. **Co³⁺:** remove one $3d$: [Ar] 3d⁶, 4 unpaired.

visual.alt: Table of the configurations and unpaired electrons of Co, Co2+ and Co3+

slides.narration: Cobalt has twenty-seven electrons: argon core, three d seven, four s two, with three unpaired. When it forms a cation, the electrons leave the outermost shell first, so the two four s electrons go first and give cobalt two plus, three d seven. Losing a third electron comes from three d, giving three d six with four unpaired electrons.

slides.heading: Configurations of ions
slides.body_md: A **cation** loses electrons from the **highest-$n$ shell first**; an **anion** adds electrons to the **next vacant subshell** of the Aufbau order. Many ions reach a **noble-gas configuration**, and species with the same electron count are **isoelectronic**.

visual.alt: Table of ions with their electrons, configurations and the noble gas they match

slides.narration: Cations lose electrons from the outermost shell first. Anions add electrons to the next vacant subshell. Look at the table: sodium, magnesium and aluminium positive ions, and nitride, oxide and fluoride ions, all have ten electrons and match neon. Chloride and calcium ions match argon. Species with the same number of electrons are called isoelectronic.

slides.heading: Quick check: electrons in a transition-metal ion
slides.body_md: Remove the electrons from the outermost shell first, then count unpaired electrons.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the configuration of the neutral atom, remembering any exception. Remove electrons from the shell with the highest n first, which means the four s electrons come off before the three d electrons. Then distribute the remaining three d electrons singly among the five boxes and count the unpaired ones.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Aufbau: lowest energy first; order of increasing (n + l), lower n first when tied.
Pauli: no two electrons with the same four quantum numbers; an orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin.
Hund: single occupancy with parallel spins before pairing in equal-energy orbitals.
Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹: half-filled and filled subshells are extra stable.
Cations lose the outermost (highest n) electrons first.

rows: Order in which subshells are filled
At most two electrons per orbital
How electrons spread over equal orbitals

visual.alt: Summary table of the three filling principles

slides.narration: Summing up Part Two. Subshells fill by increasing n plus l, with lower n first on a tie. An orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin, and electrons spread over equal orbitals singly before pairing. Chromium and copper take extra stability from half-filled and filled d subshells, and cations lose their outermost electrons first.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Write n + l for each subshell before ordering; break ties with lower n.
Write configurations in the order of filling, then regroup by shell for the final answer.
For Cr and Cu, state the exception and give the half-filled or filled reason.
For cations, remove 4s electrons before 3d; for anions, add to the next subshell.
Draw boxes for unpaired-electron questions: singly first, then pair.

visual.alt: Table of common slips in Part 2 and how to fix them

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Write n plus l for each subshell before you order them. Give configurations in the order of filling and then regroup by shell. For chromium and copper, name the exception and give the reason. For cations remove four s electrons before three d, and for unpaired electron questions draw the boxes and fill them singly first.

notes.title: Quantum Mechanical Model and Electronic Configuration — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The wave equation, ψ and ψ², and the idea of an orbital
sections.body_md:
The uncertainty principle rules out a definite orbit, so the electron is described by a **wave function ψ**, obtained by solving the **Schrödinger equation** $\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$ (the derivation is not required). Acceptable solutions exist only for certain energies and are labelled by quantum numbers. The equation can be solved exactly for hydrogen and only approximately for many-electron atoms.

ψ itself has **no direct physical meaning**. **ψ²** at a point is the **probability density**; ψ² multiplied by a small volume is the probability of finding the electron in that volume; the sum over all space is 1. Where ψ² is zero the electron is never found. An **orbital** is a one-electron wave function with its own energy, size and shape; a **boundary surface diagram** encloses about 90% of the probability, since ψ² never falls exactly to zero. The **radial probability** $4\pi r^2\psi^2$ (probability in a thin spherical shell) is zero at the nucleus and peaks at a most probable distance (1 a₀ for 1s).

key_terms.definition_md: The mathematical function that describes the electron as a wave; it has no direct physical meaning.
The probability per unit volume of finding the electron at a point.
A one-electron wave function; a region around the nucleus where the electron is most probably found, holding at most two electrons.
The surface enclosing about 90% of the electron probability of an orbital.

sections.heading: 2. The four quantum numbers
sections.body_md:
Three quantum numbers arise from the wave equation, and a fourth describes spin. **Principal** $n = 1, 2, 3\ldots$ fixes the shell, the size and the energy. **Azimuthal** $l = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1$ fixes the subshell and shape ($l = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are s, p, d, f). **Magnetic** $m_l = -l, \ldots, 0, \ldots, +l$ fixes the orientation; a subshell has $2l+1$ orbitals. **Spin** $m_s = +\tfrac12$ or $-\tfrac12$. An electron is described fully by its set $(n, l, m_l, m_s)$.

An allowed set must satisfy $l \le n-1$ and $|m_l| \le l$. For example $(2, 2, 0, +\tfrac12)$ is not allowed because $l$ cannot equal $n$.

key_terms.definition_md: Whole number 1, 2, 3 … labelling the shell; fixes size and energy.
Takes values 0 to n − 1; labels the subshell and fixes the shape of the orbital.
Takes values −l to +l; fixes the orientation of the orbital in space.
+½ or −½; the two possible spin directions of an electron.

visual.alt: Table of allowed values of l, subshells, orbitals and electron capacity for shells n = 1 to 4

sections.heading: 3. What the quantum numbers tell us; counting orbitals and electrons
sections.body_md:
**Distance and size:** a larger $n$ means the electron is on average farther from the nucleus and the orbital is larger. **Energy:** the energy of a shell rises with $n$; in a hydrogen atom it depends on $n$ alone, but in a many-electron atom on $n$ and $l$ (s < p < d < f within a shell). **Shape:** $l$. **Orientation:** $m_l$. **Spin:** $m_s$.

**Counting:** an orbital holds 2 electrons; a subshell has $2l+1$ orbitals and holds $2(2l+1)$ electrons; a shell has $n^2$ orbitals and holds $2n^2$ electrons. The s, p, d, f subshells hold 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons.

key_terms.definition_md: The set of orbitals with the same n and l (for example 3p).
The set of orbitals with the same n.

sections.heading: 4. Shapes, size and orientation of s, p and d orbitals
sections.body_md:
An **s orbital** ($l=0$) is spherical and non-directional. A **p orbital** ($l=1$) has two lobes of opposite sign on either side of the nucleus separated by a **nodal plane**; the three p orbitals $p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$ point along the axes ($m_l = -1, 0, +1$). A **d orbital** ($l=2$) comes in five orientations ($m_l = -2$ to $+2$): $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{xz}$ have four lobes between the axes; $d_{x^2-y^2}$ has four lobes along the axes; $d_{z^2}$ has two lobes along z and a ring in the xy plane.

**Size** increases with $n$ for the same type (1s < 2s < 3s; 2p < 3p). For the same $n$, an s electron is on average slightly nearer the nucleus because it penetrates it more.

key_terms.definition_md: A plane through the nucleus on which ψ² = 0 (an angular node).
The two-lobed shape of a p orbital.

sections.heading: 5. Nodes and radial probability curves
sections.body_md:
A **node** is a place where ψ² = 0. **Radial nodes** (spherical surfaces) number $n-l-1$; **angular nodes** (planes or cones through the nucleus) number $l$; the **total** is $n-1$. So 1s has none, 2s has one radial node, 2p has one nodal plane, 3s has two radial nodes, 3p has one radial node and one plane, and 3d has two angular nodes and no radial node.

In a **radial probability curve** the number of peaks is one more than the number of radial nodes. The hydrogen values for the most probable distance are 1 a₀ (1s), 4 a₀ (2p) and 9 a₀ (3d); 2s has a small inner peak and a large outer peak separated by a node at 2 a₀.

key_terms.definition_md: A spherical surface at fixed distance from the nucleus where ψ² = 0; there are n − l − 1 of them.
A plane or cone through the nucleus where ψ² = 0; there are l of them.

visual.alt: Radial probability curves for 1s, 2s, 3s, 2p, 3p and 3d showing radial nodes as dashed red lines
visual.caption: Radial nodes = n − l − 1.

sections.heading: 6. Aufbau principle, (n + l) rule, Pauli’s principle and Hund’s rule
sections.body_md:
**Aufbau:** in the ground state electrons fill the lowest-energy vacant orbitals first. **(n + l) rule:** subshells fill in order of increasing $(n+l)$; if two have the same value the one with the lower $n$ fills first. This gives 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p.

**Pauli’s exclusion principle:** no two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin. **Hund’s rule of maximum multiplicity:** in equal-energy orbitals electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing, giving the maximum number of unpaired electrons and the least repulsion.

key_terms.definition_md: Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy.
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.
Orbitals of equal energy are occupied singly, with parallel spins, before any is doubly occupied.
An electron alone in an orbital.

sections.heading: 7. Configurations of elements and ions; stability of half-filled and filled subshells
sections.body_md:
Write configurations by filling in Aufbau order and grouping by shell, for example sulfur $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^4$ or $[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^4$. **Chromium** is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1$ (not $3d^4\,4s^2$) and **copper** is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1$ (not $3d^9\,4s^2$): **half-filled** ($d^5$) and **completely filled** ($d^{10}$) subshells are extra stable because of **symmetrical distribution** of electrons and greater **exchange energy**, and 4s and 3d lie close in energy.

**Ions:** a cation loses electrons from the **outermost (highest n) shell first**, so 4s electrons go before 3d: Fe is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2$, Fe²⁺ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6$, Fe³⁺ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$. An anion adds electrons to the next vacant subshell: Cl⁻ is $[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^6$, like argon. Species with equal numbers of electrons are **isoelectronic**.

key_terms.definition_md: A subshell with one electron in each orbital, such as d⁵; extra stable.
Atoms or ions with the same number of electrons.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Treating ψ as a probability; it is ψ² that is the probability density.
- Allowing l = n, or a value of mₗ outside −l to +l, in a set of quantum numbers.
- Counting n orbitals in a shell instead of n², or forgetting the factor 2 for electrons.
- Radial nodes n − l instead of n − l − 1.
- Ordering subshells by n alone, or breaking an (n + l) tie by the larger n.
- Writing Cr as 3d⁴ 4s² and Cu as 3d⁹ 4s².
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming a transition-metal cation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definitions (orbital, node, Pauli, Hund): one mark each, with the key phrase.
- Quantum-number sets: one mark for correct n and l, one for mₗ and mₛ.
- Configurations: one mark per correct configuration; one mark for the half-filled or filled reason.
- Node calculations: formula, substitution, and the numbers for radial, angular and total.

cards.front_md: What does the Schrödinger equation do?
cards.back_md: It describes the electron as a matter wave: Ĥψ = Eψ, with acceptable ψ only for certain E.
The probability density: probability per unit volume of finding the electron at a point.

cards.front_md: Does ψ itself have physical meaning?
cards.back_md: No. Only ψ² can be interpreted (as probability density).
A one-electron wave function; the region where the electron is most probably found. It holds at most 2 electrons.

cards.front_md: What is a boundary surface diagram?
cards.back_md: A surface enclosing about 90% of the electron probability of an orbital.

cards.front_md: Radial probability of a shell at r?
cards.back_md: $4\pi r^2\psi^2\,dr$; zero at the nucleus, peak at the most probable distance.

cards.front_md: Most probable distance of the 1s electron?
cards.back_md: One Bohr radius, a₀ = 52.9 pm.
Whole numbers 1, 2, 3 …; they fix shell, size and energy.
−l to +l, that is 2l + 1 values; they fix orientation.
+½ or −½ (two spin directions).

cards.front_md: Orbitals in subshell s, p, d, f?
Orbitals and electrons in shell n?
cards.back_md: n² orbitals; 2n² electrons.

cards.front_md: Electron capacity of s, p, d, f subshells?
Which quantum number tells the shape of an orbital?
cards.back_md: The azimuthal quantum number l.
The magnetic quantum number mₗ.
l must be less than n, so l = 2 is impossible for n = 2.

cards.front_md: Shape of s and p orbitals?
cards.back_md: s: sphere; p: two lobes (dumbbell) with a nodal plane.
dxy, dyz, dxz: four lobes between axes; dx²−y²: four lobes along axes; dz²: two lobes and a ring.

cards.front_md: How does orbital size change with n?
cards.back_md: It increases: 1s < 2s < 3s and 2p < 3p.
A place where ψ² = 0, so the electron is never found there.
l (planes or cones through the nucleus).
Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy.
Lower (n + l) fills first; if equal, lower n fills first.
No two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers; an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
Equal-energy orbitals are filled singly with parallel spins before pairing.
[Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹: half-filled 3d is extra stable.
[Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹: completely filled 3d is extra stable.

cards.front_md: Which electrons does a transition-metal atom lose first?
cards.back_md: The outermost 4s electrons, before 3d.
Atoms or ions with the same number of electrons, such as Na⁺ and F⁻.

questions.stem_md: A student plotting the 1s orbital of hydrogen finds that $\psi^2$ is about $0.30$ (in suitable units) at a point very close to the nucleus and about $0.02$ at a point much farther out. She concludes correctly that the electron is:

options.text_md: moving faster near the nucleus than it does at the farther point
found only at the first point and never at the second
travelling in a circular path that passes through both points
more likely to be found in a small volume near the nucleus than in an equal volume at the farther point

questions.solution_md: $\psi^2$ is the probability density, so the larger value near the nucleus means a greater chance of finding the electron in a given small volume there — option (d). A density says nothing about speed or about a path.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the wave function ψ of an electron in an atom is correct?

options.text_md: ψ has no direct physical meaning, but ψ² at a point is the probability density there
ψ is the probability of finding the electron at a point
ψ must be positive at every point of space
ψ is zero everywhere except on a circle round the nucleus

questions.solution_md: Only the square of the wave function is interpreted, as probability density; $\psi$ itself can be positive or negative — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the quantum mechanical model of the atom, an orbital is best described as:

options.text_md: a circular path in which the electron revolves at a fixed speed
a one-electron wave function, associated with a region where the electron is most probably found
a pair of electrons with opposite spins in the same shell
the surface on which the electron is certain to be found

questions.solution_md: An orbital is the wave function of a single electron; its ψ² maps the region of high probability — option (b). It is neither a path nor a certain location.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Schrödinger equation can be solved exactly for the hydrogen atom, but for atoms with more than one electron only approximate solutions are possible.
questions.solution_md: True. The electron–electron repulsion in many-electron atoms makes an exact solution impossible, so approximations are used.

questions.stem_md: The square of the wave function, ψ², at a point gives the electron ___ at that point.
questions.solution_md: ψ² is the probability density.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An electron in the 2s orbital of hydrogen is never found at a distance of exactly 2 a₀ from the nucleus.

**Reason (R):** At that distance ψ² is zero, so the probability density there is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The 2s orbital has a radial node at 2 a₀, where ψ² = 0, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A chemistry teacher says that "ψ tells us nothing directly, but ψ² does". What does ψ² represent for an electron in an atom, and why is no meaning given to ψ itself?

answer.model_answer_md: ψ² at a point is the probability density: its product with a small volume gives the probability of finding the electron in that volume. The wave function ψ is only the amplitude of the electron wave, which may be positive or negative, and no measurable quantity corresponds to it directly.

questions.solution_md: ψ² is probability density; ψ is only an amplitude.

marking_scheme.step: ψ² as probability density (probability per unit volume)
ψ is only an amplitude with no direct physical meaning

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between the orbit of Bohr’s model and the orbital of the quantum mechanical model.

answer.model_answer_md: A Bohr orbit is a definite circular path of fixed radius, whereas an orbital is a region of space in which the electron is most probably found, described by a wave function. An orbit can hold any number of electrons by the model’s rules for shells, but an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin; also, an orbit gives an exact position, an orbital gives only a probability.

questions.solution_md: Fixed path versus probability region; exact position versus probability; capacity of two electrons.

marking_scheme.step: First correct difference (path versus region of probability)

questions.stem_md: Why is an orbital drawn as a boundary surface that contains about 90% of the electron probability, instead of a surface that contains 100%?

answer.model_answer_md: The probability density ψ² falls steadily with distance but never becomes exactly zero, so a surface that encloses all of the probability would have to extend to infinity. A boundary surface holding about 90% shows the region where the electron is mostly found and has a definite size and shape.

questions.solution_md: ψ² never reaches zero, so 100% needs an infinite surface.

marking_scheme.step: ψ² decreases with distance but never becomes zero
A 100% surface would be infinite; 90% gives a definite shape and size

questions.stem_md: Four sets of quantum numbers $(n, l, m_l, m_s)$ were proposed for electrons in different atoms. Which set is allowed?
questions.solution_md: For $(3, 2, -2, +\tfrac12)$: $l = 2 \le n-1$, $|m_l| = 2 \le l$ and $m_s = +\tfrac12$ — option (d) is allowed. Option (a) has $l = n$; option (b) has $|m_l| = 2 > l = 1$; option (c) has $m_s = 0$, which is not $\pm\tfrac12$.

questions.stem_md: A teacher prepares a wall chart showing every orbital of the shell with n = 4. The chart must show how many orbitals?
questions.solution_md: Orbitals in shell $n$ $= n^2 = 4^2 = 16$ ($1 + 3 + 5 + 7$) — option (d). 8 and 32 count electrons or confuse $n^2$ with $2n^2$.

questions.stem_md: For electrons in the shell with n = 3, which list gives all the permitted values of the azimuthal quantum number l?
questions.solution_md: $l$ runs from $0$ to $n-1 = 2$, so $l = 0, 1, 2$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two orbitals of a ground-state atom have the same values of n and l but different values of mₗ. They differ in:

options.text_md: their average distance from the nucleus
the number of nodes they possess

questions.solution_md: n fixes size, l fixes shape (and node numbers), and mₗ fixes orientation, so orbitals differing only in mₗ differ only in orientation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: How many electrons in an atom can have the quantum numbers $n = 4$ and $m_s = +\tfrac12$?
questions.solution_md: The shell $n = 4$ holds $2n^2 = 32$ electrons; each of its $n^2 = 16$ orbitals has exactly one electron with $m_s = +\tfrac12$, so the number is $16$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An electron in a 4f orbital has an azimuthal quantum number l and the subshell has a number of possible mₗ values equal to, respectively:
questions.solution_md: For an f subshell $l = 3$, so $m_l$ has $2l + 1 = 7$ values — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The shell with n = 3 contains nine orbitals.

**Reason (R):** For each value of l there are (l + 1) possible values of mₗ.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = n². R is false: mₗ has (2l + 1) values for each l, not (l + 1) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student builds a model of the O shell, the shell with $n = 5$, as a set of boxes holding two electrons each. What is the maximum number of electrons the shell can accommodate?
questions.solution_md: Electrons in shell $n$ $= 2n^2 = 2 \times 5^2 = 50$.

questions.stem_md: A subshell with azimuthal quantum number l = 2 contains ___ orbitals.
questions.solution_md: A subshell has 2l + 1 orbitals, which is 5 for l = 2.

questions.stem_md: Match each quantum number with the property of the electron or orbital that it fixes.

match_right.text_md: Orientation of the orbital in space
Size and energy of the shell

questions.solution_md: n → q (size and energy); l → s (shape); mₗ → p (orientation); mₛ → r (spin direction).

questions.stem_md: Give a set of the four quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) for the single outermost electron of a ground-state sodium atom, Z = 11, and name the subshell it occupies.

answer.model_answer_md: The configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹, so the outermost electron is in the 3s subshell. For it n = 3, l = 0, mₗ = 0 and mₛ = +½ (or −½), that is (3, 0, 0, +½).

questions.solution_md: Outermost electron in 3s; (3, 0, 0, +½).

questions.stem_md: For the 4d subshell, state the values of n and l, list the possible values of mₗ and give the maximum number of electrons it can hold.

answer.model_answer_md: For 4d: n = 4 and l = 2. mₗ can be −2, −1, 0, +1 and +2, which are five values, so there are five orbitals. The subshell holds at most 2 × 5 = 10 electrons.

questions.solution_md: n = 4, l = 2; mₗ = −2 to +2; 10 electrons.

marking_scheme.step: n = 4, l = 2 and the five values of mₗ

questions.stem_md: A student lists the subshells of the third shell, n = 3. Give the allowed values of l, name each subshell, state the number of orbitals in each, and give the maximum number of electrons in the shell.

answer.model_answer_md: For n = 3, l = 0, 1 and 2, giving the subshells 3s, 3p and 3d. They contain 1, 3, 5 orbitals respectively, 9 in all (n² = 9). With two electrons per orbital the shell holds 18 electrons (2n² = 18).

questions.solution_md: l = 0, 1, 2; 3s, 3p, 3d; 1, 3, 5 orbitals; 18 electrons.

questions.stem_md: State the four quantum numbers by name and give, for each, the allowed values and the property of the electron that it describes.

answer.model_answer_md: The principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3 …) gives the shell, and so the size and energy. The azimuthal quantum number l (0 to n − 1) gives the subshell and the shape of the orbital. The magnetic quantum number mₗ (−l to +l) gives the orientation of the orbital, and the spin quantum number mₛ (+½ or −½) gives the direction of spin of the electron.

questions.solution_md: n, l, mₗ, mₛ with their values and meanings.

marking_scheme.step: n and l with values and meanings

questions.stem_md: A teacher draws the radial probability curve of the 5s orbital of an atom. Not counting r = 0, how many times does the curve touch zero between the nucleus and infinity?
questions.solution_md: These zero points are the radial nodes: $n - l - 1 = 5 - 0 - 1 = 4$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which description of the dxy orbital is correct?

options.text_md: Four lobes lying along the x and y axes, with the xz and yz planes as nodal planes
Four lobes lying between the x and y axes, with the xy plane as the only nodal plane
Four lobes lying between the x and y axes, with the xz and yz planes as nodal planes
Two lobes along the z axis with a ring in the xy plane

questions.solution_md: The dxy orbital has its four lobes between the axes, and its two nodal planes are the xz and yz planes — option (c). Lobes along the axes belong to dx²−y²; lobes with a ring belong to dz².

questions.stem_md: The probability of finding a pz electron is zero everywhere in the:

options.text_md: surface of a sphere centred on the nucleus

questions.solution_md: The pz lobes point along the z axis, and the nodal plane is perpendicular to them, the xy plane — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following orbitals of a hydrogen atom is, on average, the largest?
questions.solution_md: Orbital size increases with the principal quantum number; 4s has the largest n of the four, so it is the largest — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The radial probability curve of an orbital shows three peaks separated by two points where it falls to zero. The orbital is:
questions.solution_md: Peaks = radial nodes + 1, so two nodes need $n - l - 1 = 2$. For 3s: $3 - 0 - 1 = 2$ — option (a). 3p has 1 node, 2s has 1 and 4d has 1.

questions.stem_md: Which orbital consists of two lobes along one axis together with a ring-shaped region of opposite sign in the plane perpendicular to that axis?
questions.solution_md: The dz² orbital has two lobes along the z axis and a ring in the xy plane — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The 3p orbital has no radial node.

**Reason (R):** The number of radial nodes of an orbital is equal to (n − l).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false. The number of radial nodes is n − l − 1 = 1 for 3p, so A is false; and R omits the − 1, so R is false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The nucleus lies on the nodal plane of every p orbital, so the probability density of a p electron at the nucleus is zero.
questions.solution_md: True. The nodal plane of a p orbital passes through the nucleus and ψ² = 0 everywhere on it.

questions.stem_md: A computer plot of the 6d orbital of an atom is to be marked with its radial nodes. How many radial nodes must be drawn?
questions.solution_md: Radial nodes $= n - l - 1 = 6 - 2 - 1 = 3$.

questions.stem_md: Match each orbital with the numbers of its radial and angular nodes.
questions.solution_md: Radial = n − l − 1 and angular = l: 2p → r (0 radial, 1 angular); 3s → p (2, 0); 3d → s (0, 2); 4p → q (2, 1).

questions.stem_md: Define a node. Calculate the numbers of radial and angular nodes of the 3p orbital.

answer.model_answer_md: A node is a region where ψ² = 0, so the probability of finding the electron there is zero. For 3p (n = 3, l = 1): radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 1 and angular nodes = l = 1.

questions.solution_md: Node: ψ² = 0. 3p: 1 radial and 1 angular.

marking_scheme.step: 1 radial and 1 angular node with the rules

questions.stem_md: Name the five d orbitals and say which one has four lobes lying along the axes.

answer.model_answer_md: The five d orbitals are dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y² and dz². The orbital dx²−y² has its four lobes along the x and y axes; the dxy, dyz and dxz orbitals have lobes between the axes.

questions.solution_md: dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y², dz²; dx²−y² has lobes along the axes.

questions.stem_md: For the 4s and 3d orbitals, calculate the number of radial nodes, angular nodes and total nodes, and say which of the two orbitals has the larger number of radial nodes.

answer.model_answer_md: Radial nodes = n − l − 1, angular nodes = l and total nodes = n − 1. For 4s: radial 3, angular 0, total 3. For 3d: radial 0, angular 2, total 2. The 4s orbital has more radial nodes (3 against 0).

questions.solution_md: 4s: 3, 0, 3; 3d: 0, 2, 2; 4s has more radial nodes.

questions.stem_md: Describe the shape of a 2p orbital. State how the three 2p orbitals are oriented, and how the size of a 3p orbital compares with that of a 2p orbital.

answer.model_answer_md: A 2p orbital has two lobes of opposite sign on either side of the nucleus (dumbbell shape), with a nodal plane through the nucleus perpendicular to the axis of the lobes. The three 2p orbitals, 2pₓ, 2p_y and 2p_z, lie along the x, y and z axes at right angles (mₗ = −1, 0, +1). A 3p orbital is larger than a 2p orbital, because size increases with n.

questions.solution_md: Two lobes with a nodal plane; three axes; 3p larger than 2p.

marking_scheme.step: Two lobes with a nodal plane through the nucleus
Three orbitals along x, y and z
3p larger than 2p because n is larger

questions.stem_md: The radial probability curve of the 2s orbital shows two peaks, while that of the 2p orbital shows only one. Explain this using the number of radial nodes, and say which of the two has its main peak at the smaller distance.

answer.model_answer_md: The number of peaks is one more than the number of radial nodes. The 2s orbital has n − l − 1 = 1 radial node, so its curve has two peaks, a small one close to the nucleus and a large outer one. The 2p orbital has n − l − 1 = 0 radial nodes, so its curve has a single peak. For hydrogen the main peak of 2p is at about 4 a₀ and that of 2s at about 5.2 a₀, so 2p has its main peak at the smaller distance.

questions.solution_md: Peaks = nodes + 1; 2s has 1 radial node, 2p has none; 2p peak nearer.

marking_scheme.step: 2s: 1 node, two peaks; 2p: no node, one peak
2p main peak at smaller distance (4 a₀ against 5.2 a₀)

questions.stem_md:
(a) Calculate the number of radial nodes, angular nodes and total nodes in each of the 5s, 4p and 3d orbitals. [3]

(b) The radial probability curves of 2s and 2p are drawn on the same axes. State the number of peaks in each and explain how this is related to the number of radial nodes. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Radial = n − l − 1, angular = l, total = n − 1. 5s: radial 4, angular 0, total 4. 4p: radial 2, angular 1, total 3. 3d: radial 0, angular 2, total 2.

(b) The 2s curve has two peaks and the 2p curve has one. The number of peaks is one more than the number of radial nodes: 2s has one radial node and 2p has none.

questions.solution_md: Node numbers from the three rules; peaks equal radial nodes plus one.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Two peaks for 2s and one for 2p
(b) Peaks = radial nodes + 1 with 1 and 0 nodes

questions.stem_md: Using the (n + l) rule, which sequence arranges the subshells 3d, 4p, 4s and 5s in order of increasing energy?
questions.solution_md: $(n+l)$: $4s = 4$, $3d = 5$, $4p = 5$, $5s = 5$. The tie at 5 is broken by lower $n$: $3d < 4p < 5s$. So $4s < 3d < 4p < 5s$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The statement that an orbital cannot hold more than two electrons, and that these two must have opposite spins, follows from:
questions.solution_md: No two electrons can have all four quantum numbers equal; in one orbital n, l and mₗ are shared, so mₛ must differ — Pauli’s exclusion principle, option (b).

questions.stem_md: The ground-state atom of an element has three electrons in its 4p subshell. According to Hund’s rule these three electrons:

options.text_md: occupy one 4p orbital as a pair and one as a single electron
occupy the three 4p orbitals singly, with opposite spins
occupy a single 4p orbital with the same spin
occupy the three 4p orbitals singly, with parallel spins

questions.solution_md: Orbitals of equal energy are filled singly with parallel spins before any pairing, so the three electrons sit in separate 4p orbitals with parallel spins — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student writes the configuration of carbon as 1s² 2s² 2p² but draws both 2p electrons as a pair in one orbital, leaving the other two 2p orbitals empty. This diagram violates:
questions.solution_md: The two electrons have opposite spins in one orbital, which Pauli allows, and the order of filling is right; but equal-energy orbitals must be filled singly first — Hund’s rule, option (b).

questions.stem_md: How many unpaired electrons are there in a ground-state selenium atom, $Z = 34$, with configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^2\,4p^4$?
questions.solution_md: Only $4p^4$ is partly filled: three boxes take one electron each and the fourth pairs with the first, leaving 2 unpaired electrons — option (a). Filled 3d and 4s contribute none.

questions.stem_md: In building up the elements, after the 5p subshell has been completely filled, the next electron enters the:
questions.solution_md: The order is ... 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f ...; $6s$ ($n+l = 6$) comes before $4f$ ($7$), $5d$ ($7$) and $6p$ ($7$) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The 3d subshell is filled before the 4s subshell because the 3d subshell has the smaller principal quantum number.
questions.solution_md: False. The (n + l) value is 4 for 4s but 5 for 3d, so 4s fills first, even though 3d has the smaller n.

questions.stem_md: Hund’s rule is also called the rule of maximum ___.
questions.solution_md: Hund’s rule of maximum multiplicity.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The 3d subshell can hold a maximum of ten electrons.

**Reason (R):** In the Aufbau order the 3d subshell is filled after the 4s subshell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. A: 3d has five orbitals (2l + 1 = 5), each holding two electrons by Pauli’s principle, so ten. R: by the (n + l) rule 4s (4 + 0 = 4) fills before 3d (3 + 2 = 5). But the filling order says nothing about how many electrons the subshell can hold, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: State Pauli’s exclusion principle and use it to find the maximum number of electrons in the 4d subshell.

answer.model_answer_md: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons, of opposite spin. The 4d subshell has five orbitals, so it holds at most 5 × 2 = 10 electrons.

questions.solution_md: Statement; 5 orbitals × 2 = 10 electrons.

questions.stem_md: State Hund’s rule and give one reason why electrons stay unpaired in the 2p subshell of nitrogen.

answer.model_answer_md: Hund’s rule: in a subshell of orbitals of equal energy, electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before any pairing begins. In nitrogen (2p³) the three electrons stay in separate 2p orbitals because electrons in different orbitals are farther apart, so the repulsion between them is smaller.

questions.solution_md: Hund statement; less repulsion when apart.

marking_scheme.step: Less repulsion between electrons in separate orbitals

questions.stem_md: Arrange the subshells 4d, 5s, 3d, 4p and 4s in increasing order of energy, giving the (n + l) value of each and stating how you decided the order of those with equal values.

answer.model_answer_md: (n + l): 4s = 4; 3d = 5; 4p = 5; 5s = 5; 4d = 6. Subshells with equal (n + l) are arranged by lower n first, so 3d (n = 3) < 4p (n = 4) < 5s (n = 5). The order is 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d.

questions.stem_md: Draw the orbital box diagram of the 3p subshell of phosphorus (Z = 15) and of sulfur (Z = 16). State the number of unpaired electrons in each and the rule that decides the arrangement.

answer.model_answer_md: Phosphorus 3p³: ↑ ↑ ↑ (three boxes, one electron each), 3 unpaired. Sulfur 3p⁴: ↑↓ ↑ ↑ (the fourth electron pairs in the first box), 2 unpaired. The arrangement follows Hund’s rule: the orbitals are occupied singly with parallel spins before any pairing.

questions.solution_md: P: 3 unpaired; S: 2 unpaired; Hund’s rule.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the Aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity. [3]

(b) Write the electronic configuration of the element of atomic number 16, draw the box diagram of its outer subshell and say how many of its electrons are unpaired. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Aufbau: electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available first. Pauli: no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin. Hund: equal-energy orbitals are occupied singly with parallel spins before pairing begins.

(b) 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4 (sulfur), [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴. Outer 3p box diagram: ↑↓ ↑ ↑, with 2 unpaired electrons.

questions.solution_md: Three principles; sulfur configuration, boxes, 2 unpaired.

questions.stem_md: The ground-state electronic configuration of nickel, Z = 28, is:
questions.solution_md: Nickel follows the Aufbau order with no exception: 2 electrons in 4s, then 8 in 3d, giving $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^8\,4s^2$ — option (c). Only Cr and Cu among Z = 21–30 are exceptions.

questions.stem_md: A sample of manganese(II) sulfate is analysed. The ground-state configuration of the Mn²⁺ ion (Z = 25) is:
questions.solution_md: Mn is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^2$. The cation loses the two outermost $4s$ electrons first, leaving $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of species is isoelectronic?
questions.solution_md: S²⁻ has 18 electrons and Ca²⁺ has 18, both [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ — option (c). Na⁺ has 10 but Cl⁻ has 18; O²⁻ has 10 but Mg has 12; F⁻ has 10 but K⁺ has 18.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best explains why a copper atom has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ and not [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²?

options.text_md: A completely filled 3d subshell is extra stable, because of symmetrical distribution of electrons and greater exchange energy
The 4s orbital in copper can hold only one electron
The 3d subshell has a lower energy than the 1s subshell in copper
Copper has one electron fewer than the Aufbau order requires

questions.solution_md: Shifting one 4s electron into 3d completes the d subshell, which has extra stability from symmetry and exchange energy — option (a). The 4s orbital can hold two electrons; the other statements are false.

questions.stem_md: Among the ions Cr³⁺, Fe³⁺, Zn²⁺ and Cu⁺ of the first transition series, which has the greatest number of unpaired electrons in its ground state?
questions.solution_md: Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons; Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³ with 3; Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰ with 0; Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰ with 0 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A vanadium(II) salt is dissolved in water. Z = 23 for vanadium. How many unpaired electrons does the V²⁺ ion have in its ground state?
questions.solution_md: V is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^3\,4s^2$; V²⁺ loses the two $4s$ electrons to give $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^3$, with three singly occupied $3d$ orbitals: 3 unpaired electrons.

questions.stem_md: A chlorine atom has atomic number 17. Using its ground-state configuration, find the total number of electrons it has in p orbitals of all shells.
questions.solution_md: Chlorine is $1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^5$: $2p^6$ and $3p^5$ give $6 + 5 = 11$ electrons in p orbitals.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The ground-state configuration of chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.

**Reason (R):** A half-filled d subshell has extra stability because of symmetrical distribution and greater exchange energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the extra stability of the half-filled 3d subshell is why one 4s electron moves to 3d, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ground-state chromium atom has six unpaired electrons.

**Reason (R):** The ground-state configuration of chromium is [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ has five singly filled 3d orbitals and one 4s electron, six unpaired. R is false: the configuration [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² would give four unpaired electrons and is not the actual configuration — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Write the ground-state configurations of copper (Z = 29) and of the Cu²⁺ ion, and explain why the copper atom does not have the configuration predicted by the Aufbau order.

answer.model_answer_md: Copper: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; Cu²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁹, the outer 4s electron and one 3d electron having been lost. The Aufbau order predicts [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s², but one 4s electron moves into 3d so that the 3d subshell is completely filled; a filled subshell is extra stable because of symmetrical distribution of charge and greater exchange energy.

questions.solution_md: Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; Cu²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁹; filled 3d is extra stable.

marking_scheme.step: Filled 3d subshell: extra stability (symmetry, exchange energy)

questions.stem_md: Write the configurations of manganese (Z = 25) and of Mn²⁺, and explain why Mn²⁺ is more stable than Mn³⁺ in terms of the 3d subshell.

answer.model_answer_md: Manganese: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; Mn²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵. Mn³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁴. Mn²⁺ has a half-filled 3d subshell (five unpaired electrons), which has extra stability from symmetrical distribution and exchange energy, so it is more stable than Mn³⁺, which has the less stable 3d⁴ arrangement.

questions.solution_md: Mn [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; Mn²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵; half-filled 3d is stable.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: extra stability of half-filled subshell

questions.stem_md: Write the configurations of N³⁻, F⁻ and Mg²⁺ (atomic numbers 7, 9 and 12), state how many electrons each has, and say what these three ions have in common.

answer.model_answer_md: N³⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; F⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Mg²⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Each has 10 = 10 = 10 = 10 electrons and the neon configuration, so they are isoelectronic.

questions.solution_md: All have 10 electrons, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; isoelectronic with neon.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the electronic configurations of chromium (Z = 24) and copper (Z = 29), and explain why each differs from the order predicted by the Aufbau principle. [3]

(b) Write the configuration of the Cr³⁺ ion and give the number of its unpaired electrons. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. The Aufbau principle predicts [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² and [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s². One 4s electron moves into 3d in each, giving a half-filled d⁵ subshell in Cr and a completely filled d¹⁰ subshell in Cu, which are extra stable because of symmetrical distribution of electrons and greater exchange energy; 4s and 3d are close in energy.

(b) Cr³⁺: [Ar] 3d³ (both 4s electrons and one 3d electron are lost), with 3 unpaired electrons in the three 3d orbitals.

questions.solution_md: Cr and Cu configurations with reasons; Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³, 3 unpaired.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Predicted configurations differ; one 4s electron moves to 3d

questions.stem_md:
An element X in the first transition series forms a 2+ ion whose 3d subshell is exactly half filled. Its atom has the configuration with two electrons in the 4s subshell.

(a) Find the atomic number of X by writing the configuration of the X²⁺ ion and of the atom. [2]

(b) Give the symbol of X, the number of unpaired electrons in its atom and in the X³⁺ ion. [2]

(c) State the electrons that are lost first when X forms its cations and why. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A half-filled 3d subshell is 3d⁵, so X²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵. Adding back the two 4s electrons gives the atom [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s², which has 18 + 5 + 2 = 25 electrons, so Z = 25.

(b) X is manganese, Mn. The Mn atom, [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s², has 5 unpaired electrons (five 3d and none in the paired 4s); Mn³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁴ with 4 unpaired electrons.

(c) The outermost 4s electrons are lost first, because they belong to the shell with the highest n, which is the outermost shell.

questions.solution_md: Z = 25 (Mn); 5 and 4 unpaired; 4s lost first.

questions.stem_md:
(a) For the electrons in the 3p subshell, write the values of n and l and list the possible values of mₗ. [2]

(b) How many different sets of the four quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) are possible for the 3p subshell? Write any two of them. [2]

(c) Show that the same subshell in the n = 2 shell, 2p, has the same number of sets, and say what quantum number distinguishes the electrons of 2p from those of 3p. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) n = 3 and l = 1; mₗ = −1, 0, +1.

(b) 3 values of mₗ × 2 values of mₛ = 6 sets, for example (3, 1, −1, +½) and (3, 1, 0, −½).

(c) 2p also has l = 1 with three mₗ values and two mₛ values, so 6 sets; they are distinguished by the principal quantum number n (2 against 3).

questions.solution_md: 3p: n = 3, l = 1, mₗ = −1, 0, +1; six sets; 2p differs by n.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is the Schrödinger wave equation, and what do ψ and ψ² stand for? [2]

(b) For the 1s orbital of hydrogen, the radial probability is zero at the nucleus and has a single maximum. Explain why the radial probability is zero at the nucleus although ψ² is largest there. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It is an equation, Ĥψ = Eψ, that describes the electron as a wave; its acceptable solutions are the wave functions ψ. ψ has no physical meaning by itself, and ψ² at a point is the probability density.

(b) The radial probability is the probability of finding the electron in a thin spherical shell, 4πr²ψ² dr. At the nucleus r = 0, so the volume of the shell, which is proportional to r², is zero, and the probability is zero even though the density ψ² is greatest there. As r increases ψ² falls but the shell volume rises, so the product passes through a maximum at about 1 a₀ and then decreases.

questions.solution_md: Ĥψ = Eψ; ψ² is density; radial probability includes the r² volume factor, so is zero at r = 0 with a maximum at 1 a₀.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Equation describing the electron wave, solutions ψ
(a) ψ² as probability density; ψ no meaning
(b) Radial probability = 4πr²ψ² dr, shell volume ∝ r²
(b) Zero at the nucleus although ψ² is largest
(b) Maximum where falling ψ² and rising volume balance (about 1 a₀)
